title: Odile and the Interior
premise: After their mother's funeral, Vesper Eriksen returns to the family's decaying coastal house to settle the estate, cataloging silences instead of possessions. Behind a wardrobe they find a bundle of undelivered letters—written by their mother to a woman named Odile, whom Vesper never knew existed. Following the letters to a shuttered artists' colony where their mother once lived, Vesper uncovers a love sacrificed to duty and an inheritance quietly stolen by their uncle, whose grip on the family fortune depends on that theft staying buried. As the house is sold out from under them and Odile's health fails, Vesper must choose between preserving their own invisibility and claiming a found family that rewrites everything they inherited; in the end, they deliver the final letter themselves and walk away from the estate with nothing but the truth—and Odile.
about_author: Odile Whitlock is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging other people's unfinished correspondence before writing her own. She lives near the northern coast, where she collects wardrobes she refuses to open.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Vesper Eriksen, POV. A week after the funeral, Vesper methodically catalogs the house: rooms, objects, and every sentence their mother never finished. The emotional beat is numb grief disguised as competence, until the list itself begins to feel like an accusation—that Vesper was also something unsaid.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Vesper, POV. Clearing the mother's bedroom for the estate sale, Vesper pries loose a panel behind the wardrobe and finds forty-one letters, all addressed to 'O,' none sent. The beat is vertigo: the careful inventory shatters as Vesper realizes the silence had an author, an audience, and a name.

chapters.title: Forty-One Winters
chapters.summary: Vesper, POV, interleaved with excerpts of the letters spanning decades. Reading chronologically, Vesper watches a young woman fall in love at the Meridian Colony and then choose, letter by letter, not to send word. The beat is intimacy with a stranger—the mother Vesper meets on the page is unrecognizable and magnetic.

chapters.title: Uncle Aldous's Ledger
chapters.summary: Vesper, POV. At the will reading, Uncle Aldous presents immaculate accounts and a quick sale offer; when Vesper mentions the colony, his pen stops moving. The beat is first dread—power shows its face only when someone looks too closely, and Vesper has just looked.

chapters.title: The Road to Meridian
chapters.summary: Vesper, POV. Abandoning the sale paperwork, Vesper drives north to the derelict colony, following a return address scrawled inside one envelope. The beat is fear sharpening into resolve: for the first time, Vesper chooses the unknown over the tidy, leaving the house unlocked behind them.

chapters.title: Odile
chapters.summary: Alternating Vesper and Odile POV. In a cottage above the frozen bay, Vesper meets Odile Halvorsen—eighty-three, sharp-tongued, expecting no one. Odile confirms the love and reveals what it cost: her paintings, her name on the deed, her thirty years of waiting. The beat is recognition across a wound.

chapters.title: What the Deed Says
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Odile gives Vesper her own archive: forged signatures, a coerced quitclaim, Aldous's fingerprints all over the colony's stolen land. The beat is fury tempered by tenderness—Odile never wanted revenge, only a witness, and now she has one who shares her blood.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Vesper, POV. Aldous arrives at Meridian unannounced, offering Vesper the house, the money, and erasure of the letters if they hand over Odile's archive. Standing between the two halves of their inheritance, Vesper refuses. The beat is the novel's moral hinge: duty finally defined on Vesper's own terms.

chapters.title: Everything Delivered
chapters.summary: Vesper and Odile, alternating POV. Vesper mails all forty-one letters plus a forty-second of their own composition, then files the deed challenge as Aldous's lawyer descends on the colony. The beat is climax and release: the silence is broken publicly, irreversibly, and the house goes up for auction to pay for the fight.

chapters.title: The Interior
chapters.summary: Vesper, POV, spring. The estate is lost, Aldous is exposed and diminished, and Vesper lives in Odile's cottage learning to paint badly while Odile teaches them to stay visible. The beat is quiet resolution: inheritance redefined—not what we're given, but what we refuse to keep silent.
